subject: phoenix
pitch:
Category: Fantastical creature.
Subject: phoenix rising from embers.
Style: your choice. Pick an unexpected, striking visual style that suits this subject (not the obvious one), name it in a comment at the top of the module, and commit to it everywhere.
reasoning:
I need to plan this module carefully since I can't test the code directly, so I should be precise with the SDK's API. For the visual concept, I'm leaning away from an obvious fiery phoenix toward something more unexpected—like a stained-glass cathedral window with lead-came lines and jewel tones, or maybe a papercut kirigami lantern style.

Settling on a cloisonné enamel aesthetic: a gilded phoenix with gold wire cell outlines filled with jewel-toned enamel in turquoise, ruby, amber, and cobalt, rising from a bed of glowing embers. I'm designing the feathers as extruded cards with SVG textures carrying gold outlines and enamel fills, using unexpected color pairings like teal and magenta against the gold and ember orange, with glow effects for the fire. For the pose, I want the bird standing upright with wings spread, legs planted in a small ember mound rather than floating, keeping it grounded in the scene.

Now I'm sketching out the skeletal structure -- defining a hips root joint and a spine chain running from the tail base up through the chest and neck to the head, with the body tilted upward at roughly a heraldic angle, wings spread outward in a display pose, and a flowing tail draping back down into the embers.

Still defining joints...

I'll just use absolute model coordinates with simple offset helpers rather than wrestling with directional word semantics. For the head shape, I'm picturing a stylized phoenix: a rounded skull, with upper and lower beak pieces built as curved swept shapes attached to the head and jaw joints respectively.

For the eyes, I'll place decal graphics on the head surface using a surface-hit helper that positions them by azimuth and elevation, giving them a gold ring accent and automatically orienting to the surface normal. Then I'm planning a crest of several flame-shaped plumes extending from the back of the head, each outlined in gold.

For the plumes themselves, I'll extrude teardrop silhouettes that curve back and taper into a point, varying their size and tilt, with smoothing and a gold-to-ruby-to-magenta gradient, all anchored to the head bone.

For the body, I'm thinking of sweeping a tapering radius profile along the spine chain, starting thick at the chest around 0.2 and narrowing to about 0.08 near the tail base.

I'm planning the spine sweep path from hips up to chest with keyed radii for smooth tapering, then continuing into the neck with overlapping radii and rounded caps -- and for the body surface I want to use a scales-style paint to fake cloisonné enamel cells with gold outlines over turquoise and cobalt base colors.

For color, I'll countershade the body: teal/cobalt scales on the back versus ruby/amber scales on the belly and chest, all outlined in flat gold. Now I'm moving on to the wings, which need an arm chain of shoulder-elbow-wrist joints with fanned primary and secondary feathers built as double-sided textured cards showing gold-outlined cloisonné feather patterns.

For the actual geometry, I'm working out how to orient extruded feather shapes using b.extrude on the wing chain, figuring out which axis represents the feather's direction versus its width so each flat feather lies correctly in the wing plane.

Designing feather outline coordinates...

SVG textures for eyes, feather cards, chest emblem decal, and ember stones with runes, aiming for about six total. Now I'm working out the wing structure — shoulder, elbow, wrist joints raised in a V-pose, with primary feathers fanning from wrist outward and secondaries trailing along the forearm.

Reconsidering scale: a 4.4m span feels too large for the phoenix, so I'm dialing it back to roughly 3.6m total with wrist position and primary feather length adjusted accordingly. I'm also defining the wing's tilt (~25° raised) and working out the local plane and normal vector so feathers extrude correctly along the span and perpendicular directions.

I'm sketching a helper function that places each feather at a given origin and direction, orthogonalizing the direction against the wing's normal so the cross products line up properly, then setting up the bone chain for shoulder-elbow-wrist on each wing.

With three names and three points, I realize the chain gives joints at shoulder and elbow spans plus a tip joint at wrist. For feather attachment I'm thinking primaries should rigidly follow the wrist tip bone while secondaries follow the forearm (elbow-to-wrist span), and I might add a few extra digit joints to support primary feather fanning.

Each primary joint parents to the wrist, positioned there, aimed along the direction of its feather group's spread — inner, mid, and outer bundles. For coverage I'm adding arm tubes (thicker near the shoulder) plus shingled covert feather rows over them, estimating roughly 30 feather/skin parts per wing for about 60 total across both wings, then moving on to the tail structure.

For the tail, I'm planning a chain of a few long plumes curving from the hips down toward the ground, built as ribbon membranes between two tapered bezier curves rather than simple tubes, so I can paint colour bands, gold edges, and scalloped chevron patterns along their length using along/across coordinates.

Still defining tail plume geometry...

Checking the cross product confirms the side vector works fine as long as the tangent isn't perfectly vertical. Now I'm working out a tapering function for the plume width, shrinking it near the tip with a power curve.

I'll clamp widths to a minimum so the plume tips don't collapse into degenerate triangles, and build each feather as a catmull-sampled polyline with a handful of rows and columns for a thin double-sided membrane. For decoration, I'm planning an eye-spot ocellus motif near the tip, painted as concentric rings radiating from a center point past 70% along the plume's length.

Now I'm designing the ember mound the phoenix stands on: low-poly glowing stones with dark cracks, flame cards, and ash/charred logs at the rim, with leg IK positioning the feet into the embers so the bird's lowest points still touch the floor at y=0.

Working out leg structure next — thigh, tibia, tarsus, three forward toes and a back toe with golden talons...

Naming the leg joint names and parenting them to the hips, then sweeping the leg chain with feathered amber thigh coverings and golden scaly tarsus texture. I'm working out how to add toes sprouting from the foot bone, considering whether to use simple spikes or small two-joint digit chains for each toe.

For the toe design, I'll build 3-joint chains per toe (base, mid, tip), parented to the foot joint, giving 4 toes per side times 2 sides times 3 joints each—24 joints total, which keeps the overall skeleton budget around 80 joints once spine, neck, head, wings, legs, and tail are tallied. Each toe chain gets swept with tapering radii and a sharp talon spike at the tip, and I'm placing the foot position relative to the mound's ground height.

I'm working out the toe tip positions sinking slightly into the mound surface, with front toes splayed at angles and a backward hind toe, then shaping the mound itself as a lathed cone profile that tapers from a wide base to a flatter top where the feet rest, before deciding on a dark charcoal paint treatment for the stone.

For the glow effect, I'm separating out individual ember chunks as small glowing icosahedra scattered across the mound surface in orange and yellow, since paint alone can't produce glow — these stay within a reasonable part budget. I'm also planning flame card elements licking up around the mound using stylized flame textures with glowing edges to match the overall decorative style.

I should limit the flames to a ring around the mound's radius so they don't obscure the phoenix itself, leaning outward for visual flow. For the glowing parts of the bird, I'm considering what should emit light — the chest sun medallion, crest flame tips, and eyes — likely using decals since their glow derives from the texture's own colors rather than the material.

For the jewelry, I'm planning a cloisonné-style gold collar with embedded gems around the neck, a gold crown band, octahedron ruby gems that glow, and gold anklets, talons, and beak detailing. The chest medallion will use a torus ring plus a decal of a sun emblem with rays in gold, ruby, and yellow tones, positioned on the front chest surface.

Now I'm working out how to place that decal correctly using surface-based positioning around the chest center point, accounting for the body's forward tilt and normal direction. I'm also thinking about adding breast feather detail by scattering small low-poly feather cards across the chest region for a plumage effect, roughly a hundred or so small cards to keep the triangle count reasonable.

For texturing those feather cards, I'm debating whether to use a grayscale drawing tinted by the underlying paint color versus separate pre-colored textures per color variant, since I want gold outlines to stay distinct rather than getting muddied by multiplicative tinting -- leaning toward making dedicated colored textures (teal, ruby, amber) each with their own gold outline baked in.

I'm setting up texture lists for different body regions, using a weighted array for the back and a separate set for the chest, then generating each via a feather texture function that takes a few fill colors. For scattering the cards onto the body, I'm filtering by surface normal and position to separate chest from back regions, then setting flow directions so the feathers shingle downward and backward with the right lean and bend angles.

I'm thinking through how card orientation relative to flow direction affects what the viewer sees from the front versus the sides, settling on a steeper lean around 70 degrees so the cards lie closer to the surface while still showing their face. I'm also deciding to keep the painted body as a base layer with cards added on top for silhouette texture, even though it's somewhat redundant, and extending card coverage to the neck and head regions with smaller feathers. Now I'm starting to define the texture list, beginning with an eye-shaped phoenix marking.

Listing out the remaining textures: flame, feather, and crest cards in teal, ruby, and amber tones, a sun medallion, and rising spark cards near the embers, each with glow effects. I'm also sketching out the paint layers beyond textures, including body cloisonné patterns, belly cells, a root-to-tip feather gradient, plume detailing, gold tarsus scales, beak coloring, and an ash charcoal mound, before starting to define the feather paint function itself.

Still writing feather paint function...

Setting paintSize to 2048 keeps lines crisp within a reasonable atlas budget, and I'll limit flat colors to a small palette like gold and ink since paints don't count against that cap. Now I'm sketching out the imports needed for the build.

Defining the gold and ruby palette constants...

Still writing feather paint logic...

Writing feather extrusion function...

Now I'm wrestling with the TypeScript typing for the outline array since it mixes plain coordinate pairs with sharp-corner markers, trying to figure out whether to import an OutlinePoint type from the SDK or just define a union type myself.

I'm checking the smoothing and bevel parameters won't cause issues at the sharp tip corner, verifying everything stays inside the build() closure as inner helpers, and confirming that passing a Vector3 for direction and y-axis extrusion is valid.

Now I'm laying out the feather outline with its base at the origin and leaf extending in +x, then moving on to designing the wing geometry — placing shoulder, elbow, and wrist points to create a raised "V" shape, and checking that the total wing height plus the phoenix's body height gives a reasonable overall scale.

Actually for a resting pose with extended wings, I'll reduce the upward angle to around 23-28°, repositioning shoulder, elbow, and wrist coordinates accordingly, then working out how primary feathers fan from the wrist with varying lengths and angles, and defining the wing plane's normal vector to give it a slight forward-up tilt.

Working out feather fan geometry...

Still working out the normal sign flip — for s=-1 the cross product points the wrong way, so I need a check that negates n when its y-component is negative, ensuring the feather plane stays consistently oriented regardless of sweep direction.

But I realize dir pointing straight back makes cross degenerate, so instead I should orthogonalize against a reference wing-normal vector that's always well-defined unless parallel to dir. Now I'm setting up the primary feather list — 9 feathers at the wrist with angles φ_i sweeping from the outermost feather pointing roughly forward.

I'm defining lengths, widths, and angular spread per feather, plus small vertical offsets between feathers to prevent z-fighting where they overlap at the base.

Now I'm planning the bone joints for the primary groups—three joints each controlling a trio of feathers, attached at the wrist. For secondaries, I'm spacing them along the forearm between elbow and wrist, sweeping their directions backward with slight outward variation.

Working out angles and bone attachments for secondaries, tertials, and scapular feathers, then layering upper surface covert rows that shadow the primaries and secondaries with shorter, offset feathers.

For the color palette, I'm going bold: a fire-meets-jewel mix where primaries blaze crimson-amber-yellow at the tips, secondaries shift teal-cobalt-violet, coverts pop magenta/ruby, and the body carries teal-cobalt on the back with ruby on the chest—tail plumes finishing in emerald-teal with ocelli accents.

I'm sweeping tubes along the arm chain with tapering radii from shoulder to wrist, painting them with a cloisonné scale pattern in ruby/crimson/magenta outlined in gold, and adding a small gold claw spike at the wrist joint plus gilded leading edges on the wings.

Now I'm mapping out the neck and head geometry, curving the neck path forward in an S-shape from the base up to the head joint, then sizing the head as a slightly flattened sphere oriented along the beak direction.

Writing beak geometry...

Still shaping the beak curves...

Now I'm placing the eye decals using spherical coordinates around the skull's center, positioning them symmetrically at an azimuth offset with slight elevation to sit naturally on the face.

For the brow arches, I'm figuring out a swept gold path above each eye, computing offset points from the eye hit location and draping them onto the skull's curved surface so they hug the geometry instead of floating above it.

I'm adding a glow effect to the eye decal, then moving on to the head crest — five flame-shaped plumes extruded along an S-curve and tilted toward the back of the head, positioning their bases along the top-back skull line.

Laying out crest plumes as a planar fan in the yz-plane, so they appear thin edge-on from the front but broad from the side, with a center cluster of five and two more offset laterally for a slight splay.

Working out the cross product for the perpendicular direction, I realize the curl orientation flips depending on which order I take the cross product -- I need the tip curling backward rather than forward, so I'll flip the sign to get the perpendicular vector pointing the right way.

For the crest coloring, I'll reuse the feather paint function with a gold-to-flame gradient and chevron patterns, and add tiny glowing gem spheres at each plume tip as an ornamental detail. I'm placing the plume origins along the head surface with slight offsets per feather index, and now thinking about adding a ring of cheek tufts around the neck for extra texture.

Writing the gold gorget collar...

I'll stick gems using the nearest surface hit so they orient outward, with a hot ruby glow color. For the chest medallion ring, I realize a flat sweep won't conform to the chest's curvature, so I should drape the closed ring points onto the skin surface instead to avoid floating or clipping.

Now I'm working out the tail chain attachment -- it needs four points spanning from the hips joint backward, and I need to confirm that the spine chain's root actually starts at the hips point so the tail parents correctly off that same joint.

I realize the zero-length bone issue between hips and spine1 since they share coordinates, so I need to offset them slightly—placing hips at one position and starting the spine path a bit higher and forward to give the bone real length.

Similarly for the tail chain, I shift tail1 away from hips to avoid another zero-length bone, settling on separate small offsets for each.

Now I'm working through the body mesh sweep, defining radii at each point along the spine to shape width and depth for the rump and torso.

Testing the taper function at t=0, 0.5, and 1 to confirm it produces a rounded bulge that narrows at the tail end — but I'm finding the math doesn't clamp cleanly at t=1, giving a zero radius instead of the small taper I want, so I need to adjust the formula.

Setting up the chain sweeps for the body, neck, and tail sheaths with tapered radius functions, then wiring the tail plumes to attach along the tail chain's bone structure.

Writing plume bezier curves...

Setting varied tip heights so the lowest ones meet the floor near the mound base while others curl upward like flame tips. For the ribbon edges, I'm sampling points along each bezier curve and computing perpendicular offsets using the tangent crossed with the up vector, tapering the width with a sine curve so it's thin at the base and widens along the length.

Now I'm defining the paint function for the plume membrane, mapping ocellus spots onto an across/along coordinate space so they sit at a fixed position along each feather-like ribbon, with the local width scaling the ellipse shape accordingly.

Still defining plume geometry...

Alternating crimson/gold for odd plumes should look striking. I'll skip the tail gem and trailing-edge flame cards, and work out the ember mound as a lathed charcoal-mottled ash base attached to the hips bone so it moves with the root.

Scattering ember stones across the mound's surface using varied dodecahedron geometries with flat shading, randomizing colors between orange, yellow, and red and sizes via the stick scale option...

I'm also planning charred logs leaning against the mound's edge, using rod geometry with charcoal coloring, plus thinking about a ring of flame cards positioned around the mound using frame placements.

Now I'm working out flame cards oriented to lean outward radially, around 16 of them scattered at varying radii with glow applied, plus adding some floating spark diamonds scattered randomly within a cylindrical volume above the scene.

Positioning sparks to avoid intersecting the wings, keeping them small and numerous with random radial and height placement. Now I'm shifting to the eye texture, sketching an almond-shaped phoenix eye with a gold lid ring, amber gradient iris, slit pupil, and a highlight for the side decal in SVG.

I need to figure out the mirroring logic for the eye flick orientation depending on which side of the head it's on, then move to setting up a radial gradient for the iris and starting the flame texture shape.

Writing SVG flame path...

Checking stroke widths render cleanly at 256px size, then moving on to designing a diamond four-point star for the spark element.

Still drawing feather chevrons...

I'll define a featherTex function with two color params so the outer vane and inner tip patch can differ, scaling up to a 128px canvas with thicker strokes, then move on to designing a sun medallion with a gold ring, triangular rays, and a ruby center disc.

Writing the ray loop and glow...

Now I'm thinking through the tarsus scale painting and leg detailing, using sweep-based ring anklets around the joints.

I'm placing torus-shaped gold anklet bands along the leg bones, positioned between known limb points, plus scattering ruby feather cards over the thigh surface for a trouser effect. Then I'm defining the rig's joint roles -- spine, neck, head, jaw, tail, wing, leg, toe -- to set up the skeletal hierarchy.

I'm establishing joint creation order with hips as the root, then building head and jaw joints that aim toward specific points relative to the neck chain, followed by mirrored wing chains for left and right sides using positional offsets.

Now I'm checking the wing shoulder placement against the chest/spine curve to make sure the wing roots align reasonably with the body geometry rather than floating away from it.

I'm computing the arm sweep radius profile tapering slightly along the wing length, and working out the elevation angle from shoulder to wrist (~24°) to set the wing's directional normal vector for orienting the surface properly.

Now I'm defining a helper function to compute feather direction from heading and elevation angles, letting primaries droop with increasing elevation toward the tips, then setting up the wrist position as the anchor point for the primary feathers.

Working out each primary's angle, elevation, and length so the fourth feather ends up longest, mimicking a real eagle's wing silhouette, and checking the resulting tip positions look plausible.

Now I'm turning to the secondary feathers, placing them along the forearm and upper arm with angles stepping from around 62° to 97° and lengths tapering slightly along that span.

I'm positioning feathers along the arc-length of the wing chain, using the joint position to split shoulder versus elbow sections, then offsetting each layer slightly along its normal to avoid z-fighting between overlapping prisms while keeping their thin thickness from intersecting.

For the coverts, I'm working out whether placing them a few centimeters above the primary base along the normal creates an acceptable shingled look or just makes them float awkwardly over the base feathers.

For secondary coverts and lesser coverts, I'm sketching out origins, lengths, and angles for another couple rows layered near the arm, then tallying up rough part counts — roughly 50-plus feather parts per side, over a hundred total, plus body parts — and thinking through how to group primaries and coverts under shared joints by index.

Then I'm estimating counts for arms, tail, legs (toes, talons, bands), head, crests, feather cards, and ember stones — landing around 260 parts total — and sanity-checking triangle budgets for feathers, membranes, and cards to make sure the mesh density stays reasonable. I'm starting to work out the hip and leg joint positions relative to the spine's base coordinates.

For the leg IK, I'm computing the distance between the hip joint and foot target against the sum of segment lengths, confirming the leg will bend into a natural bird zigzag with the knee forward and ankle back. I'm setting up a limb function that takes the root, target, segment lengths, and bend direction to return the chain of joint points (thigh, shin, tarsus, foot tip), and adjusting the mound height and foot target y-position accordingly, then planning toe placement with three forward toes at spread angles plus a hind toe pointing backward.

Now I'm working out the toe geometry: each toe gets a short polyline from the foot joint outward and slightly downward to form a claw shape, using small offsets to curve the tip, then sweeping a thin golden bone shape along that path for the digit and adding a spike for the talon tip.

I'm mirroring the toe angles across left/right using the sign, and setting hind toes to point backward. I'm also sweeping the thigh through the leg chain with a radius profile that's thick near the hip and tapers down toward the lower leg, giving a feathered, muscular silhouette.

Now I'm planning gradient color bands along that sweep, blending thigh color into gold toward the tarsus, then scattering feather cards on the thigh and spine by filtering sweep points above a certain height.

Scattering continues for chest ruff and back cards, filtering by surface normal direction to separate front from back, with distinct flow vectors, lean angles, sizes, and counts for each region, plus assigning different texture sets to each card group.

Head gets a gradient-like texture using layered color scales. Now I'm starting to write out the full builder module, defining the phoenix structure with its paint canvas size and a vector helper function.

Building the skeleton...

I notice the neck's starting point nearly coincides with the spine's endpoint, which means the chest bone might end up with near-zero length — I should check whether that's intentional or needs adjusting.

Setting up the tail chain with four points, which gives three spans plus a tip bone, and that looks correct. Now I'm defining the body sweep that wraps the spine chain with the body radius and paint color.

For the body paint, I'm layering countershade coloring between back and belly scale patterns, using teal/cobalt/emerald tones on top and ruby/crimson/amber underneath, both with gold edges, blending them softly at the border where they meet.

Now I'm figuring out how to orient the chest-facing region correctly given the body's tilt — since the torso axis leans up and forward, the chest/belly surface actually faces forward-and-down rather than straight down, so I need a normal direction like (0, -0.6, 0.8) to properly capture that front-facing patch for the ruby coloring.

I'm defining the custom paint function using a dot product of the surface normal against this forward-down direction, thresholding it to split belly cells from back cells, and adding a thin gold boundary band where the value sits near the threshold. The neck will reuse the same body paint and taper smoothly from the body's wider radius down to a narrower one.

Now I'm sweeping the tail path with a tapering radius using the body paint, then setting up wing loops for left and right sides. I'm also planning a feather helper function, a gold collar loop around the neck joint, a medallion ring, and decal placement for a sun emblem on the chest using a hit point's normal and a default world-up orientation.

I'm also considering eye placement to avoid crest overlap and sketching small cheek plume feathers that sweep back using the feather paint.

Now I'm defining a feather helper function that extrudes an outline with parameters like thickness, bevel, smoothing, and bone attachment, then using it to build the wing assembly by chaining joint points for shoulder, elbow, and wrist on each side.

Defining wing points...

Now I'm working out feather paint colors per wing layer, starting with the primaries and figuring out whether the tips should fade to pale yellow.

I'm sketching a "flame wings" palette: primaries going ruby-crimson-amber-yellow, and considering cooler secondaries like teal, cobalt, violet to contrast the fire tones with jewel-like interiors. Coverts get a magenta-ruby-crimson gradient with a smaller gold row underneath, and each feather needs its own paint instance since length varies and paints get baked per feather into the sheet.

I'm defining tail plume colors that alternate between emerald/teal/cobalt and ruby/crimson/amber, then moving to legs — writing a limb function call with root position, segment lengths, and bend directions for the inner joints, followed by building the leg chain as a polyline with knots feeding into a named joint chain parented at the hip.
